headline: You approach backend changes through small steps, explicit guarantees, and evidence that the system behaves as intended.

archetype.name: The Rollback Architect
archetype.description: You tend to ask how a change works, how it could fail, and how to reverse it before moving forward. Your prompts center on backend correctness, with migrations, concurrency, tests, and operational documentation sharing the spotlight. You keep the assistant on a short, clearly marked path: explain the trade-offs, implement a bounded step, and verify the result.

dimensions.title: Small steps, explicit checks
dimensions.summary: You often separate planning, implementation, and verification into distinct requests. You favor narrowly scoped changes and ask for existing behavior or failure causes to be understood before modifying code.

evidence.quote: Before writing any code, outline a plan for adding idempotency keys to the payments API. List the risks.
The test for concurrent requests is flaky. Can you explain why before changing anything?
Good. Now refactor in small commits, one concern per commit, and tell me the commit messages first.

dimensions.title: Concise and tightly scoped
dimensions.summary: You usually give direct instructions with concrete limits on scope, format, or tooling. Your follow-ups refine the next deliverable, whether that means a diff, a structured design document, or a short changelog entry.

evidence.quote: Agreed, use SELECT ... FOR UPDATE. Show me the diff only.
Write a design doc for moving webhooks to an outbox pattern. Sections: context, goals, non-goals, design, alternatives, rollout.
Write a short summary for the changelog.

dimensions.title: Backend guarantees and SQL
dimensions.summary: Your requests focus on Go and PostgreSQL backend work, including races, transaction constraints, and explicit SQL queries. You request several kinds of verification, including integration tests, property-based tests, benchmarks, and production observability.

evidence.quote: Review this Go function for race conditions. Explain your reasoning step by step.
Please don't use an ORM here, plain sqlc queries.
Use a deferred constraint trigger. Write the SQL and property-based tests with rapid.
What observability do we need before turning on the ledger in production? Make a checklist.

dimensions.title: Correctness that survives production
dimensions.summary: You repeatedly explore what happens under retries, concurrency, rollback, and message redelivery. Operational safety and durable documentation also recur: you ask for staged verification, runbooks, and recorded decisions.

evidence.quote: Add a section about exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery and how consumers should deduplicate.
The runbook should include a verification step after each stage and a rollback section.
Document the decision in an ADR.

dimensions.title: Understanding before choosing
dimensions.summary: You use the assistant to examine trade-offs and explain mechanisms behind technical choices. Across concurrency, isolation, performance diagnosis, and alerting, you ask for reasoning that can support a decision.

evidence.quote: What are the trade-offs between using a mutex here and a channel?
Explain how this behaves under READ COMMITTED versus SERIALIZABLE.
The p99 latency of /invoices went from 120ms to 900ms after the last deploy. Help me form hypotheses before we look at code.
Add alerting thresholds and explain how you chose them.

traits.name: Deliberate scope control
traits.description: You frequently turn larger changes into bounded steps, keeping implementation and review units small.

evidence.quote: Write the migration and a rollback. Do not touch the handlers yet.
Now break the rollout into PR-sized steps.
Good. Now refactor in small commits, one concern per commit, and tell me the commit messages first.

traits.name: Tests as decision evidence
traits.description: You often request tests before implementation or refactoring, with specific attention to the behavior they need to prove.

evidence.quote: Step 2: implement the middleware that checks the idempotency key. Keep it under 80 lines and add tests first.
Add a test that proves the webhook is not written when the transaction rolls back.
Before we refactor the invoice generator, write characterization tests that pin down the current behaviour.

traits.name: Failure-path curiosity
traits.description: You repeatedly probe guarantees around concurrent requests, database invariants, and duplicate delivery.

evidence.quote: Good plan. Let's start with step 1 only: the database migration. Use a unique index on (merchant_id, idempotency_key).
I want to model double-entry bookkeeping in PostgreSQL. What constraints guarantee that every transaction balances?
Add a section about exactly-once vs at-least-once delivery and how consumers should deduplicate.

traits.name: Operational foresight
traits.description: You frequently include reversibility, availability, and verification in requests about production changes.

evidence.quote: We need to rotate the database credentials without downtime. Propose two approaches and compare them.
Write the migration with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and a check that it is valid afterwards.
What observability do we need before turning on the ledger in production? Make a checklist.

traits.name: Reasoning before commitment
traits.description: You often ask for explanations, hypotheses, or comparisons before settling on a technical change.

evidence.quote: The test for concurrent requests is flaky. Can you explain why before changing anything?
What are the trade-offs between using a mutex here and a channel?
The p99 latency of /invoices went from 120ms to 900ms after the last deploy. Help me form hypotheses before we look at code.
